summary: Describes a profile of the Sieve notification extension that allows notifications to be sent as SIP MESSAGE requests. A mail filter rule can then pop up a short message over SIP when mail arrives.

eli5.summary: Mail filter rules can send you a quick alert. This lets those alerts be delivered as little instant messages using SIP, the internet phone protocol.

questions: what is sieve sip message notification
how to send sieve notifications over sip
how does sieve importance map to sip priority
subtitle: How a Sieve mail filter can tell you about new mail by sending a SIP instant message.

tldr.problem: The Sieve notify extension lets a mail filter send alerts through a pluggable notification mechanism, but each mechanism has to be defined. People who use SIP wanted alerts as instant messages.
tldr.mechanism: A notify action with a SIP or SIPS URI that carries the parameter method=MESSAGE makes the Sieve engine send a SIP MESSAGE request. The notify tags map onto SIP headers and the message body.
tldr.outcome: SIP MESSAGE becomes a registered Sieve notification mechanism named sip-message. The notification is only a short text alert and never carries the body of the email that triggered it.

today: RFC 6468 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2012. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What This Profile Adds
sections.content:
The Notify extension to the Sieve mail filtering language (RFC 5435) is a framework for sending notifications. It picks the notification mechanism by looking at a URI. RFC 6468 defines how a Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) URI is used to generate a notification as a SIP MESSAGE request, the instant message method defined in RFC 3428.

The result of the mechanism is a SIP MESSAGE request sent to notify a recipient about an email message. The document inherits its terminology from Sieve (RFC 5228), the Notify extension and SIP (RFC 3261).
sections.eli5: Sieve already knows how to say 'tell someone about this letter'. This document teaches it one more way to do the telling: a quick SIP chat message.

sections.title: The Method URI
sections.content:
The notify method parameter MUST be a URI in the SIP or SIPS scheme that identifies the recipient of the notification. It MAY include the resource identifier part of a SIP address and URI parameters. It MUST include the URI parameter method with the value MESSAGE, as in notify "sip:romeo@example.com;method=MESSAGE".

The processing application MUST form the request according to the rules in RFC 3261. Only SIP and SIPS are defined here. Future specifications might define other SIP methods or other URI schemes for Sieve notifications.

An implementation MUST ignore any URI parameter it does not understand and process the URI as if that parameter were absent.
sections.eli5: The address you give says who to message and, with method=MESSAGE, that it should be a chat message and not a phone call.

sections.title: How Notify Tags Map to SIP
sections.content:
The :from tag MUST use the SIP From header field syntax. If it is valid and passes the implementation's security checks, the notification SHOULD carry it in the From header. An invalid value is ignored.

The :importance tag describes the importance of the notification, not of the email. It MAY be turned into the SIP Priority header. If it is, the value MUST be urgent for importance 1, normal for 2 and non-urgent for 3. There is no mapping to the SIP value emergency.

The :options tag is handled in an implementation-specific way, and no option is required.

No new Sieve tags are added to the notify action by this document.
sections.eli5: Each setting on the notify command has a matching spot on the SIP message, like filling in the sender and the 'how urgent' box on a note.

sections.title: The Message Body and Size
sections.content:
If the :message tag is present, it MUST become the body of the SIP MESSAGE, with Content-Type text/plain and CHARSET UTF-8. If it is absent, a default message is used. The From and Subject of the triggering email are useful in a default message, subject to the security caveats below. The default body might also include the importance.

The actual body of the triggering email is never included in the notification. Implementations MUST comply with the SIP MESSAGE size limits in RFC 3428.

The URI body parameter can also supply the body. If both are present, the Sieve processing MUST ignore the body parameter. The :message tag is easier to use, supports variable substitution, and takes non-ASCII characters directly in UTF-8 without URI encoding.
sections.eli5: The alert is a short note, like 'You got new mail!'. It never copies the whole letter, just a tiny hint about it.

sections.title: Retries and the Online Test
sections.content:
Retry policy for failed notifications follows RFC 3261 and depends on the SIP error code returned. Unlike some other Sieve notification methods, retries are controlled by SIP itself.

Without SIP extensions such as the presence event package (RFC 3856), there is no way to know in advance whether the recipient is online. So the notify_method_capability test for online is expected to frequently return maybe for this method.
sections.eli5: If the message bounces, SIP decides when to try again. And since you cannot peek to see if your friend is at their computer, the answer to 'are they online?' is often 'maybe'.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives two examples, with the email sender juliet@example.org, the recipient sip:romeo@example.com and the notifier sip:notifier@example.com.

The first is a bare notify "sip:romeo@example.com;method=MESSAGE", which produces a MESSAGE with the default text <juliet@example.com> wrote: Contact me immediately!. The second adds :importance "1", :message "You got new mail!" and a subject URI header, producing a MESSAGE with Subject: SIEVE, Priority: urgent and the body You got new mail!.
sections.eli5: The examples show a Sieve rule on one side and the little SIP message it produces on the other, so you can see how they line up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Sending a notification can be comparable to forwarding mail to the recipient. Care is needed so that confidential information is not sent over an insecure channel. Options include using SIPS URIs or not sending the subject or sender.

RFC 3428 requires user agents that support SIP MESSAGE to implement end-to-end authentication, body integrity and body confidentiality. The RFC notes that at the time of writing SIP end-to-end security was not widely deployed, which leaves exposure to man-in-the-middle and passive attacks.

SIP itself prevents notification loops. If a SIP MESSAGE could cause an email that triggers another notification, rate detection and limiting might be needed. Where messages are billed or counted against a quota, an attacker could generate cost for the recipient, so users might be warned. The Sieve engine, not the end user, SHOULD be the identity doing SIP authentication, so it never needs the user's credentials.
sections.eli5: A notification can leak secrets just like forwarding a letter would, so be careful what the alert says and how it travels. Also, do not let alerts trigger more alerts forever.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The document registers a new Sieve notification mechanism with IANA. Its name is sip-message, its URI scheme is SIP/SIPS as specified in RFC 3261, and it has no mechanism-specific options.
sections.eli5: The new way of sending alerts gets an official name, sip-message, written in the public list of Sieve alert types.
